title: Rafi and Cora's Choice Adventure
markdown:
The first sunbeams, soft and golden, peeked through Rafi’s window and nudged him the way a friend does when there is somewhere to be. He popped out of bed with a bounce, feet barely touching the floor.

Downstairs, Cora the jackdaw sat on the kitchen counter, grooming shiny black feathers. Bright eyes, like tiny polished stones, watched a dust mote dance in a sunbeam. “Morning, Speedy,” she cawed, a cheerful rasp. She hopped onto Rafi’s shoulder, claws tickling his shirt. “Ready to go? Or ready to trip over your own shoelaces?”

Rafi clapped, a quick happy sound. “Ready. Ms Lin has a package. Very important. Very breakable. We need it at the Great Clock Tower before her client arrives. That’s noon.” He checked his watch. The numbers glowed. “Not much time.”

Ms Lin came in holding a small box wrapped in soft velvet, tied with a fancy knot. “This is for Professor Chronos. His special time-keeper. It keeps time from getting mixed up.” A wink. “And remember: the fastest path isn’t always the clearest. There are shortcuts, and confusing spots that slow you down. Pick the path with the smoothest flow.”

Rafi took the package as if it were a bird. “Got it. Trust us.”

They dashed out. Rafi a whirl of energy, Cora a smart black shadow on his shoulder. The town was just waking. Birds sang happy songs from the trees. Bakeries sent yummy smells of warm bread into the cool morning air. Cobblestones, still damp with dew, sparkled like little jewels. A cart rattled somewhere. A shop bell rang once, then again. Rafi tucked the velvet box closer, as if the morning itself might jostle it.

They stopped where four streets met. “Three main stretches to the Clock Tower,” Rafi said, notebook already out. “Market Street, the Riverbank, then the Whispering Woods. We have to pass all three, in that order. But each stretch splits.” He drew as he talked. “Market can go through the busy shops, or past the quiet bakery. Riverbank can go by the water, or through the park. Woods can be a quick bumpy track, or a longer shady lane.”

He listed them. Market-shops. Market-bakery. River-water. River-park. Woods-track. Woods-lane. Pencil still. “Whoa.”

A tangle of yarn. Too many ways. How could they find the fastest when there were so many to check? A little knot of worry tightened in his tummy. The Clock Tower, usually so friendly, seemed very far away. The package felt heavier.

Cora hopped from his hair to his arm and looked at the messy drawing. Head tilt. Sharp eyes seeming to solve it. “Squawk. Rafi, look. You don’t pick one street and stop. You pick Market, then River, then Woods. Each pick opens the next. It isn’t a list. It’s branches. A tree growing everywhere at once.”

Rafi blinked. Looked at Cora, then at the notebook. She was right. Not a shopping list of paths. A network of choices. He took a deep breath of crisp morning air. “You’re brilliant, Cora.” A happy rush. “That’s it. It isn’t just adding. It’s multiplying. If each stretch has two choices, it isn’t two plus two plus two. It’s two times two times two.” He counted on his fingers, then on the page. Eight complete routes. Eight ways to be early, or late.

He drew it again: a thick line for their starting point, then two Market branches, and from each of those two River branches, and from each of those two Woods branches. A little tree of mornings. He followed one path with his finger: bakery, then the water, then the dirt track. Smooth, few turns, no market crush, no park picnic-block. He checked another: shops, then park, then shady lane. Longer. Extra corners. A third: bakery, park, track — a kink that would cost minutes. A fourth: shops, water, lane — pretty, and slow.

“See,” he said, pointing to a neat spot where many lines met. “If we take Market Street past the old bakery, it connects perfectly to the Riverbank path by the water. From there, the quickest Woods dirt track, without extra turns. We only make three main choices, but the paths we could have taken branched out so much. Eight combinations. By picking this sequence, we skip the longer, trickier routes that would make us late.” He traced the chosen path. A confident smile. “This is it. This is the one.”

They dashed. Feet flying over cobblestones. They zoomed past the busy market stalls without entering them, hugging the bakery’s warm wall instead. They went alongside the sparkling river, not the park’s slow loop where someone was already laying out a picnic cloth. The Whispering Woods path was fast, a blur of green and brown, bumpy but honest. Cora leaned into the wind and did not offer a single shoelace joke.

The Great Clock Tower’s hands pointed to 11:58. Perfect. Ms Lin was already there, smiling with relief. “You made it. Wonderful work, both of you.”

Rafi handed over the package. “Cora helped. She showed me how the choices multiply. Three pairs of socks and two shirts isn’t five outfits. It’s three times two. Each independent choice multiplies the rest. Combinatorics.”

Cora puffed her chest. “Combinatorics!”

Ms Lin chuckled, warm. “The clever way possibilities combine. Useful. You solved a puzzle today.” She tucked the velvet box under her arm. “The world is full of them.”

Black wings fluttered. Rafi’s step was determined. They raced into the bright morning, hearts thumping, already wondering how many other mornings were hiding in the branches they had not taken.
characters: Rafi (a young technician), Cora (a jackdaw), Lin (a supervisor)
